title: A Social Media Quality Review of Popular Sinusitis Videos on TikTok
screen_reason: Content analysis of 220 sinusitis TikTok videos (from #sinus, #sinusitis, #sinusinfection, searched 29-30 January 2023). Beyond the quality instruments (PEMAT-AV, JAMA, GQS), every video was coded factual vs nonfactual against expert verification - 'information validated through a literature review and consultation with an expert in rhinology' - and the paper itself equates misinformation with educational-but-nonfactual videos. Table 1 gives the counts, so a share of items judged inaccurate against an external ground truth is available: CONTENT. The purely scale-based quality outcomes are recorded as a QUALITY row / notes only.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language TikTok videos; US-based investigators, University of Chicago)
estimates.date: Searched 29-30 January 2023; videos published 2020-2023 (71.0% posted in 2022, 15.4% in 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of educational sinusitis TikTok videos that were nonfactual (the paper's own definition of misinformation: educational but nonfactual)
estimates.value_raw: Education type - Nonfactual 49 (36.0%) of 136 educational videos
estimates.denominator: 136 of the 220 included sinusitis videos that were categorised as educational (intent to teach viewers); the 220 came from the first 155 videos returned for each of three hashtags (465 initial, 245 excluded as duplicates, non-English, off-topic, no audio, or deleted)
estimates.definition: Video coded nonfactual: it 'discussed nonvalidated information', where factual meant 'discussing information validated through a literature review and consultation with an expert in rhinology (C.R.R.)'
estimates.misinfo_def: "Videos with misinformation (educational but nonfactual) were deemed harmful, while videos with factual information were beneficial."
estimates.page_loc: p. 4, Table 1, 'Education type' rows (all videos, then by uploader type); Results, 'Video Content'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Factual status determined by validation against a literature review plus consultation with a rhinology expert among the authors (C.R.R.); two independent reviewers (R.D., D.F.) assessed the videos with a third reviewer (S.C.) resolving disagreements; no kappa or percentage agreement reported
estimates.moderator_quote: Using the hashtags "sinus," "sinusitis," and "sinus infection," we searched TikTok posts from January 29 to 30, 2023. ... One independent researcher collected the first 155 videos recommended by TikTok's standard search algorithm for each hashtag.
estimates.notes: This is the row that matches the paper's own misinformation definition (educational but nonfactual = harmful), so it is preferred over the all-video nonfactual share. breadth coded 'misleading' rather than 'false' because the numerator is 'nonvalidated information', which is broader than demonstrably false. A whole-sample version is derivable from verbatim counts: 49 nonfactual educational videos / 220 included videos = 22.3%; not made the headline value because 36.0% is the printed figure. Sample is rank-truncated (first 155 per hashtag) and English-only.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language TikTok videos; US-based investigators)
estimates.measure_type: % of ALL sinusitis TikTok videos (educational or not) coded nonfactual, i.e. not conveying expert-validated information
estimates.denominator: All 220 included sinusitis TikTok videos, including the 84 non-educational ones (comedy 28, lifestyle 76, marketing 2 across the whole sample)
estimates.definition: Video coded 'Factual: No' - it did not discuss information validated by literature review and rhinology-expert consultation
estimates.misinfo_def: "Factual videos were defined as those discussing information validated through a literature review and consultation with an expert in rhinology (C.R.R.), while nonfactual videos discussed nonvalidated information."
estimates.page_loc: p. 4, Table 1, 'Factual' rows (all videos, then by uploader type); Results, 'Video Content'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same instrument as the CONTENT row: expert-rhinologist plus literature-review validation, two reviewers with a third adjudicating, no reliability statistic reported
estimates.moderator_quote: Neutral videos were noneducational videos, such as comedy or lifestyle/acceptability videos that did not claim to share nonfactual educational content.
estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY, not CONTENT, and excluded from prevalence: with the all-video denominator a wholly true or claim-free item can land in the numerator - 49 of the 84 non-educational videos (comedy, lifestyle vlogs, marketing) are counted 'nonfactual' simply because they convey no validated information, and the authors themselves call such videos neutral rather than harmful. It is kept as the broad definition variant of the CONTENT row (44.5% vs 36.0% in the same sample) to document how much the number moves with the denominator.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Uploader-type subgroup shares were NOT given rows although the abstract headlines them: among educational videos, nonfactual rates were 53.2% for nonmedical influencers (33/62; i.e. 46.7% factual), 29.0% for lay individuals (9/31), 16.3% for medical professionals (7/42); among all videos, nonfactual was 55.7% (59/106) for nonmedical influencers, 46.4% (32/69) for lay, 15.5% (7/45) for medical professionals. These are source-type subgroups of the extracted rows, not a country/platform/measure split, so the main figures were kept per the collapse rule; an adjudicator wanting a source-type moderator can lift them directly from Table 1. (2) Scale means with no share are excluded per the instructions: GQS 2.70 (SD 0.92), understandability 0.80, actionability 0.50, JAMA 0.50, harm/benefit 0.22. In particular the harm/benefit scale is reported only as a mean, so the % of videos scored harmful (-1) is NOT recoverable, even though 'harmful' is the paper's misinformation flag. (3) Content-category shares (medical advice 51.8%, lifestyle 34.5%, comedy 12.7%, marketing 0.9%) and educational share (61.8%) are not veracity judgements. (4) Exposure figures exist (330,771,103 views, 1,127,415 shares over 220 videos) but views are never broken down by factual status, so no view-weighted EXPOSURE row is possible. (5) No CONCENTRATION statistic is reported, though the paper notes 183 unique uploaders for 220 videos and that nonmedical influencers had fewer unique uploaders per video. (6) 'Almost half of the videos were published by nonmedical influencers' (48.1%) is an uploader share, not a misinformation share.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a rank-truncated, English-only convenience sample: first 155 videos returned by TikTok's search algorithm for each of three hashtags on 29-30 January 2023 (465 videos, all collected within 24 hours to limit algorithmic drift), 245 excluded (138 duplicates, 44 non-English, 47 off-topic, 10 no audio, 6 private/deleted), leaving 220. Two independent reviewers coded each video with a third resolving disagreements; factual status validated by literature review plus an author rhinologist; standard instruments (PEMAT-AV, JAMA criteria, GQS, harm/benefit) used for quality; no inter-rater reliability statistic (kappa or % agreement) is reported anywhere; analyses by Wilcoxon, Fisher exact, Welch t, ANOVA and random-intercept regression. Uploader-type classification relies on self-declared professional status and a 10,000-follower cut-off.
rob.item6_quote: Factual videos were deﬁned as those discussing information validated through a literature review and consultation with an expert in rhinology (C.R.R.), while nonfactual videos discussed nonvalidated information.
rob.item10_quote: More than half of all videos were categorized as factual (55.5%, n = 122); however, the presence of factual content signiﬁcantly differed among uploader types (lay individual: 53.6%, 37/69; nonmedical inﬂuencer: 45.3%, 48/106; medical professional: 84.4%, 38/45; P < .001)
